text:
DNF my first marathon. Quit after 2-miles.

I've been training since the beginning of the year. I did two Pete's base aerobic plans going from 15 to 30 mpw and then from 30 to 45 mpw. After that I did the full 18/55 program missing only 3 runs early on. I've ran almost 1500 miles this year. Everything was great until the last week when I got a runny nose and a bit of a dry throat.
I thought it was mostly irritation from a cheap Chinese KN95 mask (which contributed to this). However, my symptoms were mild - no fever, no body aches, RHR normal. I did a 3.5 mile recover run the day before and I felt ready.
On the day of the marathon, I again felt pretty good. It was a cold 32F weather. I started running and I noticed my breathing felt a lot more labored than it should at that effort. I kept going. I tried reducing the speed. I took a break at 1.5 mile. I tried running again at a slower speed but I could tell that this was not sustainable and that something was off. At mile 2, I decided to quit and walk back. I noticed I had wheezing in my chest. It turned out I had a mild acute asthma attack because I had a mild cold and combined with the cold air trigger the asthma attack.
I felt fine the rest of the day and today. I plan on running another marathon in 3-weeks.
I just thought I share my story because there are a lot of stories about people running with an active cold. Not always a good idea. There is always another marathon.
EDIT: Thank you for all the support. I didn't expect this much support. This is one of the reasons I love dedicated running communities because people uinderstand what you are going through.
I had time to reflect on all of these:
I know quitting, especially, your first marathon can feel like the world is coming to an end but I accomplished a lot of great things this year that even if I don't end up running a full marathon matter a lot:
My first 5k was last December, 2025 and it was 24:50
My second 5k in March, 2026 increasing mileage to 30 mpw was 22:19.
At the beginning of the year my longest run was 6 miles. Now, I've ran multiple 21-mile runs in the hot and humid Boston summer.
I accomplished so many first like first time I hit 40mpw, first time I hit 50 mpw, first time I did 59mpw, etc. I cried so many times afterwards because I felt so proud. I never though any of this is possible. It felt like a dream.
In addition, to running, I kept serious weight training, and usually did 3-4 double days per week and even increased my RDLs to 320-340lbs for multiple reps and I am 150lbs.
I connected with many runners and fitness enthusiast and I started feeling like I am part of a community.
My base aerobic pace improved to 9:00-9:30 min/mile. At the beginning of the year it was ~12 min/mile.
I can keep going but this is enough. DNF does not mean the end of the world.

text:
First (but not my last) marathon!

First marathon in the books: 3:09:2×!
This weekend, I ran my first marathon, and I enjoyed every single kilometer!
A little background: I'm 33M. I come from a football background and used to do strength training 2–3 times a week. I hung up my football boots in the summer of 2025.
A few friends had signed up for a 15K trail race in April 2026, and I joined them. In February, I went for my first run longer than 10K, and I was hooked almost instantly. After running a few races, I eventually signed up for the Amsterdam Marathon.
I initially let ChatGPT put together a training plan for me. Thanks to this sub, I quickly realized it was rubbish. Lesson learned! Read some literature and ended up running five times a week for at least 13 weeks, consistently clocking 60–75 km per week, followed by a three-week taper.
Race day!
Did a half marathon in 1.27.3× so i thought that 3.10 would be challenging but doable. I started with the 3:10 pacers. It was pretty crowded so I dropped back about 50 meters to find my own rhythm. Which was really hars the first 10k because of the amount of runners.
The race went surprisingly smoothly. I felt good for almost the entire distance, sticking to my fueling plan with a gel every 30 minutes and a few sips of water at the aid stations.
At 27K, I suddenly got a side stitch. For a moment, I thought, Oh no, is this where my race falls apart? Thankfully, it disappeared pretty quickly, and I was back on track.
As the kilometers ticked by, I realized my goal was within reach. At 40K, I caught up with and passed the 3:10 pacers. That gave me a huge boost heading into the final stretch.
I crossed the finish line in sub 3.10 and i dodged the man withthe hammer! I couldn't have asked for a better debut, and I've definitely caught the marathon bug.
A huge thanks to everyone in this sub. I've learned so much from the advice and race recaps shared here!
What's next?
For my next marathon I'd prefer a race with a smaller field to have a little more room to find my rhythm.
I'm planning to follow a Pfitzinger training plan, most likely the 12/55 or the 18/55. I should also bring back the strength training.
Hopefully, the next training block will give me the confidence to take a proper shot at breaking the three-hour barrier. After this weekend, I'm excited to see what's possible.
On to the next one!

text:
Under 3 by the skin of my teeth!

Big goal checked off today at the Mount Desert Island Marathon!
Came in with a rough follow of Pfitz 18/85, with a strong focus on listening to my body, taking rest days when needed, and accommodating an otherwise busy schedule. Peak week was 83 miles, with marquee workouts of a 22 miler @ 7:04, 22 miles w/ 14 @ 6:36 pace, and Yasso 800s averaging 2:52 per rep. Tried to train hills but couldn’t really find anything comparable to the elevation that MDI would give me.
Weather in race day was truly pristine - 33° and sunny with minimal wind at race start. First half went quite well, coming through at 1:29:30. Fueling strategy was 1 Gu every 4 miles, a swig of Powerade at each water station every 2 miles, and then a sip from my race bottle with 2 packs of Liquid IV every other mile. Felt strong through the first half and knew than sub-3 was possible, but far from secured.
The first cracks came around 17, when I became acutely aware of how sore my quads were. The whole course was rolling hills, so there was little rest for the wicked. I was still able to grind through until 21, where the last big set of hills came in. I knew at 21 that if I could average 7:00 for the rest of the race I would hit my goal.
Cramps took hold of my hamstrings first and my calves second up the final hills. Pace slowed and navigating the course and the half marathoners became more difficult. When I got to the top of the final hills at 25, I was aching for the sweet release of death. But I also knew that I needed to push it.
The last full mile was downhill, so I sent it with reckless abandon. I was completely cramping up the last .2 and had to stop twice in the last bit for a couple seconds to stop myself from completely tying up. But with a sprint finish and a collapse at the line, I came through with a 2:59:50 and a first class trip the medical tent.
Next step is to eat a whole bunch of pizza, and then start gearing towards a BQ in the spring, this time on a flat course!

text:
Migraine success

Yesterday I completed my first ever half marathon. Previously, running anything over about 8 miles would end with me having a horrific migraine, but with some experimentation and preparation I’ve managed to avoid it. Here are the measures I took, hopefully it helps someone else:
- Pace: I used Runna to train and keep my pace. In an event it’s easy to get carried away with other runners and go too fast. The app helped me to keep it steady. I also found that starting slowly and building my pace gradually, then slowing right down for the last half mile helps.
- Eating: I had a decent breakfast, carbs and protein and then about an hour before the race began I had another banana and a jam sandwich. Once I finished I made sure to have some more to eat, particularly salty food; so a ham sandwich, pork pie, salty crisps
- Hydration: I made sure I was well hydrated before I started. I drank some electrolytes before the race, there were water stations at 3, 6, and 9 miles with an electrolyte station at the halfway; I drank at all of them. My wife was waiting at the finish line with a Lucazade Isotonic drink (this is one of the biggest effectors I think) and a big bottle of water. I also had more electrolytes.
- Fuelling: I took three SIS Isotonic energy gels on the race which I had every half hour.
- Running: I took on a slower cadence with greater stride length which felt more relaxed but maintained my pace, I was conscious to drop my shoulders to not compress my neck, I was pushing my elbows back to open my chest and breath easier. It was a bright day so I wore a baseball cap (but a really thin one so I didn’t overheat my head) and sunglasses.
There’s quite a few things there, I don’t think there was one thing that cracked it for me but a combination of everything. The lucazade immediately at the end probably helped the most though. Hopefully there’s something in there to help others with the same exercise trigger as me.

After hours of running almost without stopping, I reached the last stretch, where my friends and family were waiting for me by the roadside. All the training, the missed parties, and the 4 am alarms in summer to avoid the heat flashed before my eyes, when I was crossing the finish line. It’s an incredible feeling to know you’re capable of something like that. I’ve been so happy ever since.
Honestly, looking back, I don’t even know how I did it. My longest run was 35k, and I planned my pacing and fueling based on that run.

text:
Sold on the Three-Day Carb Load

I just ran my 33rd marathon, and somehow this was the first time I tried a three-day carb load. I had always been skeptical about whether it was really effective. I’d read articles years ago questioning the need for such a long carb-loading period so I never adapted it.
I’ve generally had decent luck with marathons. If I was properly trained, uninjured, and didn’t go out too fast, I never really bonked. Yes, the last six miles or so were always difficult and somewhat painful, but I usually managed to push through and maintain my pace.
Now that I’m 57, I’ve been looking for ways to maintain my performance as I get older, so I decided to try the three-day carb load for the first this time.
The first day did not go well. I ate too much protein, filled up, and had trouble reaching my carb target. The next day, I focused on reducing my protein, fat, and fiber intake while maximizing carbohydrates. I also started loading earlier in the day, which worked much better.
Race day turned out to be a little warm in Chicago, but I didn’t adjust my goal. I decided to go for it. My heart rate was a little higher than expected right from the start, probably because of the heat and the excitement of the race. That worried me because I thought I might crash later.
I was dreading hitting the 20-mile wall, but then it never happened. The weather was getting really warm by this time, but I barely noticed. I was completely focused on maintaining my pace through the finish. My heart rate was a little more elevated near the end, but never reached a point where I felt the need to back off.
I ended up finishing about 11 minutes under my BQ time. My second half was only 16 seconds slower than my first half, and my final mile was the second-fastest mile of the marathon.
In retrospect, I don’t think I could have run that race without the extra carb loading. I set my PR 20 years ago and didn't really come close to it this time but I think this was my best marathon performance ever. Looking back, I think the one day carb loads I used to do were severely lacking. I didn't really track, just ate pasta for two meals which I now think was not sufficient.

So in summary I've got really mixed feelings about the race. I finished with 3.25 which I'm satisfied with for my first crack, but I'm also frustrated that I left SO much time out there. text:
Integrity Over Influence: Are We Holding Fitness Influencers to the Same Standards as Everyday Runners?

A Chicago-based content creator with the Instagram handle @itsjdwill publicly posted on his story just a few weeks before the Chicago Marathon, stating, “I have dinner for anyone that can get me a bib for the Chicago Marathon.”
Apparently, going through the proper channels to secure a bib doesn’t apply when you have influence in the fitness community.
He allegedly went on to secure a bib from a friend, but not only that, PUMA also stepped up and may have asked him to wear their products during the marathon and post pictures before and after for promotional content.
The problem is that no one seems to hold these content creators to any standard. It’s very much like a baby being coddled when they do something wrong.
Bib number #71840 was reportedly registered to another individual.
The Chicago Marathon’s official rules outline the following potential consequences:
Violation
Official consequences
Running with another person’s bib
Removal from the course and possible disqualification from future events
Selling, giving away, or transferring a bib
Disqualification and/or a ban from future events for anyone involved
Finishing under an improperly assigned bib
Disqualification and removal from official results
Now, the questions are: Will these two individuals be held to the appropriate standards, or are we going to turn a blind eye again in this sport for the sake of content and likes?
As far as the brand sponsorship goes, what should happen to them? Did their team do its due diligence?
The problem I believe exists in this sport is that neither the brands nor the individuals seem to face any repercussions because it increasingly feels like a “who you know” business.
So, for everyday runners who can’t run a sub-three-hour marathon or don’t have the influence to raise significant funds for a cause, the opportunity to participate in these races can feel almost impossible.
These are people who train for months, sometimes years, hoping for a chance to stand at the starting line. Yet, when someone with influence appears to bypass the process, we’re supposed to look the other way?
The Abbott World Marathon Majors Six Star Medal will remain nothing more than a dream for many everyday runners.
And that’s what makes this so disappointing. Running is supposed to be a sport built on hard work, perseverance, fairness, and integrity. Those values shouldn’t disappear just because someone has followers, brand sponsorships, or connections.

text:
Abingdon Marathon Review (First Marathon M57)

A few notes on my first marathon, Abingdon Marathon (S.England, UK) raced on 18th October - hope this might be useful for anyone of masters age (about me: M57, 66-64kg) contemplating whether they can run a marathon!
I gave myself a New Year target to run a marathon in the year, and came into 2026 with a sketchy background of running. Mostly Parkuns in 2025, mixed up with infrequent longer runs up to half-marathon pace. I foolishly thought, with that background I could compete in a Spring Marathon with 16 weeks of training so followed a typical training plan that peaked at ~30km in April. But hell, that broke me .. and I thought there was no way I was ready for a full Marathon. Saw that Abingdon (a local Autumn marathon) was available and reserved a space for October 18th, an Autumn target made more sense.
So, after a further couple of months of base training, I picked up a new Marathon training Plan from June'26 which gave me a new plan over 20 weeks to prepare. I used Gemini AI - entered my details, target pace, background, ParkRun on Saturday, Long Run on Sunday, and a couple of runs during the working week - and it came up with a nice plan tailored to my week and target paces. Typically, I would keep my ParkRun as my tempo run (25min target), two runs in the week (Tuesd/Thurs) and a longer run on Sunday.
As things turned out, training wasn't perfect. I hit a few injuries (Calf strains), family holidays in September (meaning I missed my target Sunday long runs), and then thought I had a catastrophic injury on September 27th when I had a Grade 1 Hamstring Tear just 10km into my final long slow run. That injury gave me 3 weeks to recover, but entering taper thought it was just about possible.
Over the last 3 weeks I focused on strength training on my hamstring, and was able to return to a few short runs in the week leading to the race, but no more than 5km at target pace (5:40/km). Up until the race I had no idea whether I would be able to run 5km or 42km, or anywhere in between.
Fortunately, Abingdon Marathon is a flat race so risk of hamstring strain is reduced a bit. Weather was pretty close to ideal with temperatures around 12C, although Northerly wind picked up with wind in range of 10-16mph leading to a headwind in final few miles. The route weaved in and out of a few towns in a largely rural location, with part that contained a loop that you ran round twice. Marshalling was superb, crowds were cheering on using your name on your bib .. which really gave a nice boost and made it feel quite personal
I set my Polar watch with race pace of distance of 42.5km (allowing for distance errors) and target time of 3:59:00 to give myself a minute margin under a 4hour target. Bone-conduction earphones are a must, disqualification is threatened if ear-buds are used as parts of the route are open to traffic and marshals need to be heard to give instruction. In truth, the traffic was never a problem - the occasional cars that were passed where all considerate and the runners came first. Spotify Muse radio channel was my go to music list, which I only used when the crowd thinned out on occasions, most of the time it was nice to hear the crowd cheering you on.
For energy, I planned to use Decathlon +3hr Energy Gels that have 2:1 glucose/fructose (30g carb, 180mg salt) every 4km, so 10 gels carried in running belt with my phone. I also made up a sports drink (250ml, Active Root, 40g carbs, 567mg salt) in a soft hand-carried water bottle. I ended up taking 9 gels, one left unused, I think I missed a gel around 36km mark, in total that's about 340g of carbs and more than enough salt.
Water stations were every ~3miles and a managed to take a few gulps of water at each, and a couple of water stations provided Active Root isotonic drinks which I used to refill my 250ml. I tried to take my gels before each water station.
The start was in cracking weather. An earlier rain shower had passed, morning temperature was fresh, probably around 10C, and heart-rate was low after race started, just 124bpm in the first km, and took 5 km to reach 150 which is where I expected to be for most of the race. Those first comfortable 5km's gave me a 2 minute cushion ahead of my target time.
I checked in on myself regularly .. how was I feeling, could I keep up the pace, hamstring check, heartbeat .. and at half-marathon I was feeling quite strong.
When I hit 30km I feared the wall, but other than increasing fatigue it didn't really hit me and I mentally convinced myself it was just another 10km to go, just 2 park-runs at an easy pace.
I kept the focus on small distance targets, next water-stations, fueling, and avoiding over-stretching that hamstring. Heart rate increased to mid 150's by 10km, to low/mid 160's from about 30km. With about 5km to go, I felt my 2 min cushion was enough to ensure I could complete within 4 hours so slowed a little to ensure I didn't injure my hamstring, but was fairly confident I was going to complete. By this time, I was overtaking others who were walking or holding their own hamstrings and tried to give support where I could. The finish is a lap of running circuit at Tilsley Park in Abingdon leading to the finishing line opposite a grandstand.
My Polar Flow tracking had landed on a Training Index of 51 before the race, with a predicted time of 3:57:00. From the beginning of Feb to race date in Oct I did 141 runs, a total distance of 1540km (also cycled about 1300km from a daily easy work commute of about 13km day). For the last couple of months I'd also been using Runalyse which I wish I'd discovered earlier, and that had estimated I could also do a 3:57:00 based on my training up to the end of August and before my lack of training and injury in September kicked in which led to it predicting a slower outcome of around 4:10:00 due to the lack of long runs and distance training.
Finished with official time of 3:56:27 - pretty much spot on with Polar and Runalyse predictions, feeling quite emotional with myself at the end.
btw, I had not run any half-marathons at race pace in training, the longest segment at race pace (5:40/km) was around 10km. I'd done plenty of half-marathon distances but none faster than about 2:10:00 yet during the race my first HM split was 1:55:52.
